opus-5.5.text:
I think it will change the picture quite a lot, though maybe not in the way people first expect.

If you look at the trajectory of the past few years, a lot of things that used to require a specialized system, like a dedicated translation model, a dedicated coding model, or a dedicated customer service bot, have gradually been absorbed by the general model. Each time the base model's generalization improves, a whole layer of vertical engineering becomes unnecessary. A lot of the hand-crafted workflows, the prompt chains, the rule-based scaffolding people built around weaker models, simply stop being needed. The model can figure out the task by itself, plan, use tools, and recover from errors. So I think a large share of what today we call "vertical agents" is really compensating for the general model not being strong enough yet. As generalization improves, that compensation layer will shrink.

That said, I don't think vertical agents disappear completely. What remains valuable shifts from the "intelligence" part to the "context" part. The general agent can reason very well, but it doesn't automatically have your company's proprietary data, your internal systems, your permissions, your accountability structure, or the very long-tail domain feedback that only exists inside a particular industry. Whoever owns that environment, the data and the feedback loop and the integration into the actual workflow, still has something meaningful. But the moat is less about building a smarter model for your niche, and more about owning the environment and the distribution.

There's also an important dynamic here: the general model gets better precisely by learning from many different environments. So in some sense the vertical scenarios become training grounds for the general agent. The more diverse tasks the model sees, the better it generalizes, and then it comes back and does the vertical task better than the specialized system. That's a kind of flywheel that favors generality.

So my view is: if your vertical product's core value is "we made the model do something it couldn't quite do on its own," that's fragile, because the next generation of the base model will likely just do it. If your value is "we have unique data, unique feedback, and we sit deeply inside the user's workflow," that's much more durable. For a team like ours, the bet is on pushing the generalization of the base model as far as possible, because I believe that's where most of the long-term value accrues.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger generalization and tool use can make many vertical agents unnecessary, but it does not specifically connect this to generalizing across long-tail tools.

r002.rationale: The response mentions internal systems and workflow integration as valuable context, but does not explain that equipping a general-purpose agent with domain-specific tools gives it domain specialization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think generalization is the whole game here. If you look at why vertical agents exist today, it's mostly because the general models aren't good enough yet. Someone builds a legal agent or a coding agent or a customer-service agent, and what they're really doing is compensating for the base model's weaknesses—adding scaffolding, hand-crafted workflows, domain-specific prompts, retrieval pipelines, a lot of glue. That glue is a patch over a capability gap, not a fundamental feature of the problem.

So as generalization improves, I think a large fraction of that work gets absorbed by the model itself. We've already seen this pattern several times. A few years ago, people built elaborate pipelines for things like sentiment classification or named entity recognition, and then a sufficiently general model just did it in-context, and those pipelines disappeared. I'd expect the same thing with agents. A lot of the "vertical agent" category will turn out to have been a transitional form.

That said, I don't think it goes to zero, and I want to be precise about what remains. There are really two things that a general model can't easily get on its own. One is proprietary data and context—the internal state of a company, its documents, its tools, its customer history. The other is the interface to the real world, the integrations, the permissions, the feedback loop where the agent's actions actually change something and you can observe the outcome. Those don't come for free with better pretraining. So I think the value shifts from "we built a specialized model" to "we own the environment and the data the agent operates in." The moat moves from the model to the context.

Actually, I'd push on this a little further. The thing I find most interesting is that generalization and specialization aren't really opposites. The way we think about it at Moonshot is that strong generalization is what makes specialization cheap. If the base model has really learned how to learn—how to pick up a new tool, a new domain, a new set of constraints from a small amount of experience—then adapting it to a vertical becomes a matter of giving it the right environment and letting it get better through interaction, rather than training a separate system from scratch. So the "vertical agent" of the future might just be a general agent that has accumulated experience in a particular setting. The specialization lives in the experience, not in the architecture.

And there's a scaling argument too. Every vertical agent that's built as a separate thing has to pay its own cost for each capability. A general agent amortizes that across everything. Historically, when you get an order of magnitude more capable base model, the specialized solutions built on the previous generation mostly don't survive. I don't see a reason to think that pattern stops. So if I were building a company today, I'd be very careful about whether what I'm building is a durable asset—data, distribution, a real environment with real feedback—or whether it's a temporary workaround for a model limitation that's going to disappear in the next release.

r001.rationale: The response says a general agent can learn a new tool and domain from limited experience, and that improved generalization will absorb much of the work now done by vertical agents.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting a general agent to a vertical by giving it the right environment, including tools, and letting it improve through interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think as general-purpose agents get better at generalizing, there will be less need to build a separate agent for every task. If the same model can learn a new workflow from instructions and examples, a lot of what we currently call specialization becomes configuration rather than a fundamentally different system.

But that doesn’t mean vertical applications disappear. There’s still value in having access to the right data, integrating with the tools people actually use, and being able to verify that a task was completed correctly. A general-purpose agent might have the capability to do the work, but you still need to put it in the right environment.

So I would expect the boundary to shift. More of the intelligence comes from the general model, while the vertical layer focuses on context, integration, and reliability. The question becomes: what does your specialized system provide that the general-purpose agent can’t easily get on its own?

r001.rationale: The response says improved generalization could reduce the need for separate agents, but it does not specifically connect that reduction to generalizing across long-tail tools.

r002.rationale: The response mentions tool integration and context in vertical applications, but does not state that domain-specific tools equip a general-purpose agent with domain specialization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think better generalization will reduce the need to build a separate agent for every vertical. If a general-purpose agent can learn a new workflow from instructions and examples, then a lot of specialization can happen through context, tools, and access to the right data, rather than through training a different model.

But that doesn’t mean vertical products disappear. There’s still a lot of value in understanding the customer’s workflow, integrating with their systems, and making the agent reliable enough for a particular task. So I would separate specialization at the model level from specialization at the product level. As general models improve, we may need less of the former, while the latter remains very important.
